titleStmt.title: Chapter 5 — Ancient Foundations — Kullaba - E-Anna instances I

div.p: We first examine how the Kullaba-E-Anna dyad emerges from the deepest levels of Mesopotamian antiquity. Indeed, it seems to emerge already fully formed in the dual precincts of Uruk. In fact, the cultural and geographic structure likely emerged in the course of the city's growth, but its exact origin remains obscured by the lack of unambiguous written sources. We are going to formulate hypotheses about this origin below and then follow its evolution into the dominant religious-political model of the ancient world. In the following, the numbers in square brackets in section headings refer back to the table in Chapter 4.

div.head: 5.1 [1] Late Chalcolithic Uruk — The Architectural Birth of the Sovereignty Engine
5.1.1 Archaeological findings and developmental hypotheses
div.p: Archaeological excavations within the Late Chalcolithic city of Uruk (fourth millennium BCE) have delineated two distinct urban zones conventionally designated as sacred precincts. The first, known as Kullaba, is traditionally associated with the cult of Anu, whereas the second, referred to as E-Anna in the literature, is identified as the cultic center of the goddess InannaFor a general description of the spatial organization of the Uruk site during the Late Chalcolithic, establishing the division between the western Anu precinct and the eastern E-Anna precinct, see Hans J. Nissen, The Early History of the Ancient Near East, 9000-2000 B.C. (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1988), pp. 96-100. Nissen notes that the spatial bifurcation of these precincts physically embodied the dual administrative and cultic spheres of the early city.. The developmental trajectory of these two precincts is generally characterized by contrasting spatial logic. The primary monument of the Kullaba is the Anu Ziggurat, which was subjected to successive rebuildings until it achieved sufficient height to dominate Uruk's skyline. Consequently, the architectural hallmark of the Kullaba district is its pronounced verticalityOn the architectural emphasis on verticality in the Kullaba precinct, see Gwendolyn Leick, Mesopotamia: The Invention of the City (London: Penguin Books, 2001), p. 48. Leick highlights that the Anu precinct was characterized by an artificial mountain... a deliberate vertical thrust into the sky, projecting a static, patriarchal dominance in marked contrast to the E-Anna's horizontal spread.. The E-Anna, by contrast, is defined by its horizontality, evolving over subsequent centuries into an expansive, laterally distributed complex of cultic and administrative structures, generally interpreted as storehouses and bureaucratic centers. The backdrop to this architectural evolution was the demographic explosion of Uruk and its emergence as a regional hegemon capable of projecting cultural, if not direct political, influence over a vast geographic expanseFor a comprehensive analysis of this demographic and economic explosion, see Mario Liverani, Uruk: The First City, trans. Zainab Bahrani and Marc Van De Mieroop (London: Equinox, 2006), pp. 15-30. Liverani demonstrates that Uruk's emergence fundamentally relied on a system of unequal exchange centralized by temple institutions..

The modern scholarly nomenclature for these precincts is derived from third-millennium BCE texts, alongside the recovery of early proto-cuneiform tablets that attribute these spaces to the respective cults of Anu (Kullaba) and Inanna (E-Anna). However, this specific attribution is only considered secure for the Late Uruk period (circa 3300 BCE). The developmental context of the early to middle fourth millennium BCE remains conjectural.While the divine transfer of ownership theory—which posits that the E-Anna originally belonged to Anu before being appropriated by Inanna—is frequently considered obsolete in contemporary scholarship in favor of models emphasizing gradual, synchronous development, we maintain its conceptual validity. Notably, the Sumerian designation E-Anna (translating to House of Heavens or House of Anu) suggests that, at some juncture, this eastern precinct was also the institutional preserve of the god Anu. Later literary traditions, most notably Inanna and EnkiThe Sumerian myth Inanna and Enki recounts the goddess Inanna's journey to Eridu, where she intoxicates the elder god Enki and appropriates the me (the divine decrees of civilization), bringing them to Uruk. This narrative is widely understood as a mythological encoding of Uruk's usurpation of Eridu's ancient religious hegemony. As Kramer and Maier observe, the myth reflects an ideological transition: The myth was invented... to validate Uruk's claim to superiority over the much older and more venerable Eridu by illustrating the triumph of Inanna's dynamic priesthood over Enki's traditional authority. See Samuel Noah Kramer and John Maier, Myths of Enki, The Crafty God (New York: Oxford University Press, 1989), p. 58. and Gilgameš and the Bull of HeavenIn the poem Gilgameš and the Bull of Heaven, Inanna demands the mythical Bull of Heaven from her father, the sky god Anu, threatening to break down the gates of the netherworld and unleash the dead if he refuses. This extortion of the highest patriarchal deity is indicative of intense internal cultic friction within Uruk. Tzvi Abusch notes that Inanna's aggressive intimidation of Anu reflects the usurpation of the highest heaven by the martial goddess, signaling the E-Anna's ideological dominance over the Kullaba's traditional patriarchal structure. See Tzvi Abusch, Ishtar, in Dictionary of Deities and Demons in the Bible, ed. K. van der Toorn, B. Becking, and P.W. van der Horst (Leiden: Brill, 1999), p. 457., suggest acute rivalry, if not overt institutional hostility, between the cult of Inanna and the patriarchal cults of Anu and his predecessor at Eridu, Enki.

div.head: 5.1.2 The Traditional Interpretation
div.p: The prevailing scholarly consensus regarding the religio-political structure of Late Chalcolithic Uruk foregrounds the centralized authority of a dominant male figure, conventionally designated by modern historians as the priest-king or proto-en. Iconographic evidence from the period, most notably the Warka Vase and numerous cylinder seals, frequently depicts this bearded figure engaged in cultic, administrative, and martial activities. He is shown orchestrating the presentation of agricultural surplus and leading processions toward the goddess Inanna, establishing his ideological legitimacy as the prime mediator between the divine and the urban populace. Many scholars interpret these depictions as the earliest visual evidence of a hieros gamos (sacred marriage) ideology, wherein the leader's intimate bond with the martial-erotic goddess justifies his accumulation of unprecedented wealth and coercive powerThe identification of the priest-king and his relationship to the goddess on the Uruk Vase is considered central to understanding early Mesopotamian sovereignty. Susan Pollock highlights how this iconography served as the ideological mobilization of surplus by the temple, naturalized through the relationship between the leader and the goddess. See Susan Pollock, Ancient Mesopotamia: The Eden that Never Was (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999), p. 189.. Concurrent with this ideological performance, the E-Anna precinct evolved into a massive bureaucratic apparatus. It managed the demographic explosion and orchestrated Uruk's colonial expansion across Greater Mesopotamia by pioneering proto-cuneiform writing and advanced accounting systems. Thus, the orthodox view holds that the E-Anna successfully fused charismatic religious authority with ruthless administrative efficiencyOn the vast administrative scope of the E-Anna bureaucracy during Uruk's expansion, Guillermo Algaze explains that the E-anna precinct served as the bureaucratic heart of a massively expanding regional economy, fundamentally dependent on the centralized administration of both resources and cultic ideology. See Guillermo Algaze, Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization: The Evolution of an Urban Landscape (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2008), p. 120..

div.head: 5.1.3 Revised Interpretation
div.p: Orthodox interpretations of Uruk’s Late Chalcolithic archaeological record harbor several contentious assumptions, chief among them the uncritical application of the priest-king paradigm. In subsequent epochs of Mesopotamian history, a leader explicitly associated with Inanna-Ishtar is invariably categorized as a king, possessing the requisite martial and erotic prestige, rather than operating merely as a cultic priest or supreme scribe. It is historically probable that Late Chalcolithic Uruk was governed by martial sovereigns during various phases of its protracted, eight-century existence. However, the documented institutional rivalry between the Anu and Inanna cults renders it highly unlikely that a singular monarch could have monopolized all administrative and cultic authority. We must postulate the concurrent existence of a professional corps of priest-scribe administrators, with whom the martial leader was forced to negotiate power. It is conceivable that, periodically, this bureaucratic priesthood engaged in conflicts of varying intensity with the sovereign, occasionally resulting in deposition. This analysis posits that the martial leader of Uruk functioned as the institutional predecessor to the later lugalThe term lugal translates literally to big man and designates a martial king. As noted by Bradshaw and Head, The gods acted as celestial guarantors of the king's power, enabling him to assume the position of big man in society—as the Sumerian word for king (LUGAL, literally big man) signifies. See Jeffrey M. Bradshaw and Ronan James Head, The Investiture Panel at Mari and Rituals of Divine Kingship in the Ancient Near East, in Studies in the Bible and Antiquity 4 (2012): 1-42., whereas the administrative priest-scribe corps comprised en-priests under the direction of a figure corresponding to the later ensiThe title ensi evolved to mean governor or administrator, representing the civil authority of the city-state. Glassner observes that rulers such as Gudea used the title ensi rather than lugal no doubt to show their devotion to the gods and emphasize their administrative and religious stewardship over pure martial sovereignty. See Jean-Jacques Glassner, Mesopotamian Chronicles (Atlanta: Society of Biblical Literature, 2004), p. 73.. Consequently, we envision early Uruk's political architecture as a fundamentally dualistic leadership structure (lugal/ensi), characterized by periods of pragmatic cooperation—during which the proto-ensi functioned effectively as the vizier to the proto-lugal—interspersed with phases of intense factional rivalry.

div.head: 5.1.4 Ideological Legitimacy of the Ensi
div.p: We suggest that this early administrative governor derived his institutional legitimacy from the Anu cult, centered in the Kullaba, whose traditional roots extended back to the archaic and immemorial prototype of Enki at Eridu. Anu of Uruk and Enlil of NippurThe tripartite division of the cosmos among the three supreme male deities became a cornerstone of Sumerian theology in later millennia. Georges Roux summarizes this mythological evolution, noting that after the primordial creation, Ki and Anu mated, and Ki gave birth to the air which separated the sky from the earth... The air was named Enlil... His temple was at Nippur and considered the most important temple until the beginning of the 2nd millennium B.C. This cosmogonic framework essentially retrofitted earlier, independent city-gods into a unified theological system. See Georges Roux, Ancient Iraq (London: Penguin Books, 1992), p. 94. are likely derivative theological constructs, modeled upon the patriarchal template of Enki. The most compelling evidence for this hypothesis lies in their nomenclature and the subsequent mythological distribution of their cosmic domains. Enki translates in Sumerian as the leader (or foreman) of the Earth. This linguistic root is consistent with a developmental phase (the latter half of the fifth millennium BCE) during which Enki functioned as the solitary, supreme deity of Southern Mesopotamia—effectively the sole patriarchal manager of the land. Subsequently, Anu (the Sky) and Enlil (the air, i.e., the space between Sky and Earth) were introduced during the formative centuries of the fourth millennium BCE. It appears that the urban populations of Uruk and Nippur designated their poliad deities with newly invented yet complementary cosmic jurisdictions while structurally imitating the stabilizing, paternal persona of Enki. It is probable that during the early fourth millennium BCE, Anu and his ensi deputy governed Uruk unchallenged from the Kullaba. As demographic density intensified, the E-Anna precinct was established. As its etymology confirms, this secondary zone was originally dedicated to Anu and placed under the authority of the ensi; however, its function was overwhelmingly administrative, engineered to manage the rapidly expanding, temple-centric redistributive economy. It is possible that a newly emerged tabooization of the Kullaba sacred space made it impossible to conduct mundane everyday transactions there and that a new district, still clearly demarcated as the preserve of Anu but geographically separate, had become a necessity.

div.head: 5.1.5 Ideological Legitimacy of the Lugal
div.p: The unprecedented agglomeration of agricultural surplus within Uruk's central granaries inherently amplified the risk of external depredation by peripheral communities. To mitigate this vulnerability, a specialized martial apparatus must have emerged to defend these assets, and likely also to extract further resources from the city's expanding hinterland. The commander of this nascent military force was the proto-lugal. Inanna—initially a deity tied to village-level agricultural fecundity and storehousesFor an analysis of Inanna's earlier roots as a deity associated with the communal storehouse, agricultural fertility, and the date palm harvest prior to her later martial-erotic syncretism, see Thorkild Jacobsen, The Treasures of Darkness: A History of Mesopotamian Religion (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1976), pp. 32-35.—was subsequently co-opted into the martial sphere of this proto-lugal. Her latent, fertility-related sexual attributes were aggressively recontextualized into a sacred prostitute persona, operating within the intensely homosocial environment of the martial leader's soldiery. Her mythological association with the tavern and orgiastic rites perfectly aligns with her transformation into the patron deity of a nascent military subcultureJeremy Black, Graham Cunningham, Eleanor Robson, and Gábor Zólyomi, A cir-namcub to Inana (Inana I), in The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (Oxford: University of Oxford, 1998), lines 16-22: When I sit by the gate of the tavern, I am a prostitute familiar with the penis; the friend of a man, the girlfriend of a woman.. Serving as the divine consort of the lugal, Inanna played a foundational role in forging the ideological cohesion and morale of Uruk's early military forces. The charismatic, mimetic bond generated between commander and troops via this divine projection was likely the primary engine driving the lugal's ascent in Urukian politics. Whether this ascendancy manifested as an abrupt military usurpation or a gradual structural evolution remains obscured by the pre-literate nature of the era. Regardless, by the terminus of the Uruk period, the Inanna cult had effectively commandeered the E-Anna and its vast redistributive apparatus (still administered by the Kullaba-aligned scribe-priests), while the triumphant lugal was iconographically immortalized on the supreme register of the Warka VaseDescribing this foundational iconographic scene, Holly Pittman writes: The uppermost register depicts the figure of the priest-king, the paramount male figure of the city of Uruk, greeting the priestess of Inana. The priest-king is clad in a distinctive net skirt and accompanied front and back by acolytes bearing offerings of food and textiles. See Holly Pittman, The First Cities, in Journey to the City: A Companion to the Middle East Galleries at the Penn Museum (Philadelphia: Penn Museum, 2018), p. 58..

div.head: 5.1.6 The Crystallization of the Dual Model
div.p: The institutional evolution delineated above exposes the genesis of the dual engine of sovereign legitimation. This structural crystallization was undoubtedly non-linear, punctuated by cyclical regressions and internal contestations. Nevertheless, by the close of the fourth millennium BCE, the bipartite system had been firmly established and physically codified in the monumental mud-brick architecture of Uruk’s dual sacred precincts. By this epoch, the ideological persona of the proto-king was deeply synthesized with the purportedly paradoxical persona of InannaAs observed in Section 1.2, traditional scholarship often struggles to reconcile the seemingly contradictory elements of Inanna's persona. See Zainab Bahrani, Women of Babylon: Gender and Representation in Mesopotamia (London: Routledge, 2001), p. 140. Bahrani highlights the goddess's inherent duality and boundary-breaking nature as an authentic theological paradox, rather than analyzing it as a pragmatic ideological construct tailored to the martial requirements of the lugal.. Contextualized thus, the perceived theological paradox dissolves. It is structurally coherent for an ex-military commander turned paramount sovereign—an amplified alpha-male archetype—to project authority through a deity that synthesizes erotic allure with martial violence. Crucially, however, the sovereign and his divine female projection never entirely eclipsed the Anu cult nor the cadre of scribe-priests whose legitimacy rested upon the god's paternal authority. This bureaucratic faction invariably maintained oversight of the E-Anna's complex economic ledgers, while simultaneously fulfilling their enduring cultic obligations at the towering Anu Ziggurat in the Kullaba.

div.head: 5.2 [2] Sargon of Akkad — The Ascendancy of the Pure E-Anna State
5.2.1 Current Scholarship on the Akkadian Empire
div.p: The traditional historiography of the Ancient Near East identifies Sargon of Akkad (c. 2334–2279 BCE) as a watershed figure who decisively dismantled the localized, Early Dynastic city-state paradigm to forge the world's first (historically attested) territorial empire. Uruk in the Late Chalcolithic (see Section 5.1) is also generally accepted to have been a kind of empire, although, because it existed in a pre-literate era, Sargon's Akkad qualifies as the first unambiguously attested one. Orthodox scholarship predominantly focuses on the administrative, military, and linguistic innovations of the Akkadian dynasty. Sargon and his successors are credited with establishing the first professional standing army, centralizing land tenure, standardizing weights and measures, and initiating the gradual replacement of Sumerian with Akkadian as the lingua franca of administration and diplomacyFor a comprehensive overview of the administrative and military apparatus of the Akkadian period, see Aage Westenholz, The Old Akkadian Period: History and Culture, in Mesopotamia: Akkade-Zeit und Ur III-Zeit, ed. Walther Sallaberger and Aage Westenholz (Fribourg: Academic Press, 1999), pp. 17-117. Westenholz meticulously catalogs the bureaucratic mechanics and military innovations that underpinned Sargon's territorial conquests.. Furthermore, scholars such as Mario Liverani have extensively analyzed the Akkadian imperial project through the lens of political economy and center-periphery dynamics, interpreting Sargon's reign as a structural triumph of logistics, resource extraction, and the ideological synthesis of Sumerian and Semitic cultural matricesMario Liverani, Akkad: The First World Empire: Structure, Ideology, Traditions (Padua: Sargon srl, 1993), pp. 43-66. Liverani emphasizes the empire's structural reliance on the violent extraction of peripheral resources to fuel the metropolitan core at Agade.. In these standard interpretations, the religious ideology of the Akkadian kings is frequently treated as a secondary byproduct—a mere reflection or legitimation of pre-existing material and military realities, in traditional Marxist-materialist fashion.

div.head: 5.2.2 Divergence: The Thermodynamics of Usurpation
div.p: The dual sovereignty framework proposed herein fundamentally diverges from the orthodox socio-economic interpretation. Rather than viewing Sargon merely as a pragmatic administrative innovator, this model identifies him as the ultimate manifestation of the pure lugal-BDMB archetype—a sovereign who completely decoupled the martial-erotic engine of the E-Anna from the regulatory constraints of the Kullaba. Historically, Sargon was a usurper. Originating as a cupbearer to Ur-Zababa, the king of Kish, Sargon possessed zero legal legitimacy; he lacked the dynastic pedigree, the ancestral land rights, and the structural endorsement of the established patriarchal priesthoods (the legacy of the Anu/Enlil ensi tradition)Benjamin R. Foster highlights the structural necessity of Sargon's ideological self-invention, noting that as a self-made usurper (his name, Šarru-kīn, defensively translates to the king is legitimate), Sargon was forced to rely on personal charismatic authority rather than established dynastic institutions. See Benjamin R. Foster, The Age of Agade: Inventing Empire in Ancient Mesopotamia (London: Routledge, 2015), p. 3.. Deprived of the linguistic and bureaucratic prestige of the Kullaba, Sargon was compelled to construct his sovereignty exclusively upon the raw, contagious charismatic capital of the E-Anna. He represents the ascendancy of a purely Ishtarian state. By loudly proclaiming himself the chosen lover of Ishtar, Sargon triggered a Girardian mimetic triangle of unprecedented scale: the goddess's divine, erotic favor hyper-valorized the usurper, infecting his rapidly expanding military apparatus with a fanatic, testosterone-fueled devotion that effectively circumvented the traditional Sumerian city-state bureaucracies. Of course, in the process, Sargon forced the bureaucrat-priests to obey him and put their logistics at the service of his military endeavors, but he did not bother to seek legitimation from them. He simply terrified them into compliance. In doing so, he was not innovating, but simply walking in the footsteps of those Urukian proto-lugals who had defied the Kullaba before him. Sargon succeeded where his predecessors probably had not, but not for long.

div.head: 5.2.3 Ishtar's Lover and the Charismatic Monopoly
div.p: To sustain this overt charismatic engine, Sargon and his dynasty explicitly leveraged the existing ideology of the sovereign as Ishtar's lover (the BDMB archetype), scaled it up to a doctrine of universal martial supremacy, and started the process that would lead to the fully fleshed-out hieros gamos of later timesFor a comprehensive scholarly overview of the historical development and ideological function of the sacred marriage (hieros gamos) ritual in Mesopotamia, see Pirjo Lapinkivi, The Sumerian Sacred Marriage in the Light of Comparative Evidence (Helsinki: The Neo-Assyrian Text Corpus Project, 2004); and Jerrold S. Cooper, Sacred Marriage and Popular Cult in Early Mesopotamia, in Official Cult and Popular Religion in the Ancient Near East, ed. Eiko Matsushima (Heidelberg: Universitätsverlag C. Winter, 1993), pp. 81-96.. The famous Sargon Legend—which, while extant only in Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian copies, accurately distills the core ideological mythos of his reign—explicitly grounds his invincibility in the goddess's passion: While I was a gardener, Ishtar granted me her love, and for four and ... years I exercised kingship.For the translation and analysis of the Sargon Birth Legend and its ideological implications regarding divine selection via erotic favor, see Joan Goodnick Westenholz, Legends of the Kings of Akkade: The Texts (Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns, 1997), pp. 36-49. Sargon did not justify his empire through an appeal to cosmic law, accounting ledgers, or the righteous justice that Hammurabi would later deploy; he justified it through the unmediated, ecstatic violence endorsed by Ishtar. This generated an incredibly potent, rapidly expanding military contagion, but one that was thermodynamically unstable. Lacking the fire extinguisher of the Kullaba's stabilizing paternal structures, the Akkadian empire was forced to consume constant external conquests merely to maintain its internal mimetic cohesion.

div.head: 5.2.4 Enheduanna: The Ideological Architect of the E-Anna
div.p: The most crucial operative in Sargon’s ideological consolidation was not a general, but his daughter, Enheduanna. Installed by Sargon as the high priestess (en) of the moon god Nanna at Ur, her primary historical function was the theological synthesis of her father’s raw military power. Contrary to modern interpretations that occasionally romanticize her as an autonomous feminist icon, within the framework of the dual sovereignty engine, Enheduanna functioned as the supreme propagandist for the E-Anna paradigmZainab Bahrani notes the immense political utility of Enheduanna's appointment, arguing that her theological poetry was a highly calculated instrument of Akkadian imperial consolidation, designed to superimpose Agade's aggressive ideology over the traditional Sumerian religious landscape. See Zainab Bahrani, Women of Babylon: Gender and Representation in Mesopotamia (London: Routledge, 2001), pp. 114-118.. In her surviving hymns, Enheduanna systematically elevates Inanna from the powerful poliad deity of Uruk to an omnipotent, boundary-breaking cosmic force, thereby mythologizing the horrific physical violence of the Akkadian standing army as the divine epiphany of the goddess. Her texts brilliantly capture the contagious, terrifying mimetic escalation of the military warband:

cit.quote: Like a dragon you have deposited venom on the land. When you roar at the earth like Thunder, no vegetation can stand up to you. A flood descending from its mountain, O foremost one, you are the Inana of heaven and earth! Raining flaming fire over the Land, endowed with divine powers by Anu, lady who rides upon a beast, whose words are spoken at the holy command of An! The great rites are yours: who can fathom them?
cit.bibl: Jeremy Black, Graham Cunningham, Eleanor Robson, and Gábor Zólyomi, The exaltation of Inana (Inana B), in The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (Oxford: University of Oxford, 1998), lines 9-14.

div.p: Enheduanna explicitly weaponizes the inherently transgressive, dualistic nature of the goddess to justify the dismantling of traditional urban boundaries (city walls) by her father's forces. The annihilation of enemy infrastructure is framed not as mere secular pillaging, but as a sacred performance of the goddess's martial-erotic overdrive:

cit.quote: In the van of battle, all is struck down before you. With your strength, my lady, teeth can crush flint. You charge forward like a charging storm. You roar with the roaring storm, you continually thunder with Iškur. You spread exhaustion with the stormwinds, while your own feet remain tireless.
cit.bibl: Jeremy Black, Graham Cunningham, Eleanor Robson, and Gábor Zólyomi, The exaltation of Inana (Inana B), in The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (Oxford: University of Oxford, 1998), lines 25-30.

div.p: Moreover, she actively portrays the horrific consequences of Akkadian conquest—the reduction of populations to slavery and the imposition of systemic terror—as the inevitable punishment for failing to submit to Inanna's charismatic authority. In her myth Inana and Ebiḫ, the goddess destroys an entire mountain range merely because it refused to display mimetic deference to her majesty:

cit.quote: Against the magnificent mountain which did not bow down to me, against Ebiḫ which did not bow down to me ... I will hurl a great storm at it ... I will make its thick clouds of dust gather in the sky ... I will plant my feet on its neck.
cit.bibl: Jeremy Black, Graham Cunningham, Eleanor Robson, and Gábor Zólyomi, Inana and Ebiḫ, in The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (Oxford: University of Oxford, 1998), lines 39-47.

div.head: 5.2.5 The Thermodynamic Collapse of the Pure Red State
div.p: While the pure E-Anna engine engineered by Sargon and articulated by Enheduanna propelled the Akkadian state to unprecedented territorial hegemony, it was structurally doomed. The mimetic contagion of the Ishtarian warband can conquer, but it cannot organically govern. Because the Akkadian kings relied disproportionately on overt charismatic violence rather than synthesizing their power with the stable, bureaucratic paternalism of the Kullaba, their empire was plagued by incessant, endemic rebellions. The E-Anna engine ran dangerously hot. The logical, fatal terminus of this unchecked charismatic escalation occurred under Sargon's grandson, Naram-Sin. Dispensing entirely with the need for a divine mediator, Naram-Sin declared himself the living god of Agade—the ultimate, hubristic short-circuit of the mimetic triangleOn Naram-Sin's self-deification and its ideological consequences, see Piotr Michalowski, Memory and Deed: The Historiography of the Political Expansion of the Akkad State, in Akkad, the First World Empire, ed. Mario Liverani (Padua: Sargon srl, 1993), pp. 69-90. Piotr Michalowski analyzes how Naram-Sin's unprecedented assumption of the divine determinative marked a radical, ultimately unsustainable ideological departure in Mesopotamian kingship.. This hyper-alpha projection, completely untethered from the moderating, linguistic trust generated by the Kullaba priesthoods, eventually alienated the established religious centers and precipitated the total systemic collapse mythologized in the Curse of Agade. The Akkadian experiment empirically demonstrated that a pure, unalloyed Ishtarian state cannot indefinitely sustain itself; it necessitates the legalist-paternal glove that Hammurabi would later master.

div.head: 5.3 [3] Hammurabi of Babylon — The First Great Synthesis
5.3.1 The Post-Akkadian Pendulum and the Amorite Warlords
div.p: After Akkad's destruction by the Gutians and a brief interregnum, the neo-Sumerian Ur III state emerged. The Ur III kings attempted an ambitious constitutional synthesis, seeking to reconcile the overt self-deification pioneered by Naram-Sin with the restored paternal authority of the Kullaba, represented most prominently by Enlil at Nippur. This structural compromise was vividly dramatized through the hieros gamos (sacred marriage) celebration, conducted during one of the two annual Akitu festivals. In this highly charged ritual, the deified king, adopting the persona of the shepherd god Dumuzi, physically consummated his marriage to the goddess Inanna. While the exact mechanics of this ritual consummation remain a subject of debate—it is unclear precisely how physical the act was or who functioned as the goddess's earthly surrogate—administrative receipts from the period incontrovertibly document the construction and provisioning of an elaborate ceremonial bed for this specific purposeFor detailed discussions on the administrative evidence of the sacred marriage bed and the ideological synthesis of the Ur III period, see Walther Sallaberger and Aage Westenholz, Mesopotamia: Akkade-Zeit und Ur III-Zeit (Fribourg: Academic Press, 1999), pp. 152-156; and Jacob Klein, Three Šulgi Hymns: Sumerian Royal Hymns Glorifying King Šulgi of Ur (Ramat-Gan: Bar-Ilan University Press, 1981), pp. 32-38.. Ultimately, however, this frontal and overt synthesis of two diametrically opposed paradigms—the pure paternal legalism of Enlil fused directly with the ecstatic, Ishtarian martial-eroticism of Inanna—proved thermodynamically unstable. The ideological contradictions were too glaring to be viable in the long term, contributing significantly to the dynasty's collapse in under a century.

The geopolitical landscape of Mesopotamia following the collapse of Ur III was defined by intense fragmentation. By the early second millennium BCE, the alluvium was dominated by rival Amorite warlords ruling over fractured city-states such as Larsa, Eshnunna, and Mari. These rulers operated essentially as localized BDMB figures, heavily reliant on personal charismatic authority and martial prowess. Hammurabi of Babylon (c. 1792–1750 BCE) emerged from this volatile matrix. However, unlike Sargon, who allowed the E-Anna engine to overheat and consume his dynasty, or the Ur III kings, whose attempted synthesis was overtly blatant and contradictory, Hammurabi succeeded in engineering the first durably stable constitutional synthesis of the two ruler-legitimation modalities. He mastered the thermodynamic regulation of sovereignty by achieving balance between the explosive mimetic contagion of the Ishtarian warband and the paternal, linguistic elder-prestige of the Kullaba apparatus. This Babylonian SynthesisFor a detailed analysis of how Hammurabi successfully unified his empire by merging Amorite military traditions with traditional Mesopotamian royal ideologies of justice, see Dominique Charpin, Hammurabi of Babylon, trans. M.B. DeBevoise (London: I.B. Tauris, 2012), pp. 70-85. became the foundational template for Eurasian statecraft, anticipating the identical structural mechanisms deployed by Augustus in Rome nearly two millennia later.

div.head: 5.3.2 The Righteous Glove: Marduk, Shamash, and the Code
div.p: The most visible and enduring mechanism of Hammurabi’s rule is the famous Stele of Hammurabi, the ultimate manifestation of the Kullaba paradigm. The Stele is not a utilitarian legal code in the modern statutory sense, but rather a colossal piece of ideological propaganda designed to project the righteous ruler personaFor the interpretation of the Code as a monument of royal apologia and cosmic justice rather than applied statutory law, see Martha T. Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1995), pp. 71-75.. At the apex of the monument, Hammurabi is depicted not as a weapon-wielding warlord receiving the erotic embrace of Ishtar, but standing in reverent, pious submission before the seated sun god Shamash, the ultimate arbiter of cosmic justice. The prologue of the text explicitly grounds his authority in the mandate of Anu, Enlil, and Marduk, declaring his divine mission: to make justice visible in the land, to destroy the wicked person and the evil-doer, that the strong might not injure the weak.Martha T. Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor, p. 76. By adopting this paternalistic, protective posture, Hammurabi systematically cultivated a coalition of the meek among his subject populations. He offered them the ultimate Kullaba-esque promise: linguistic arbitration, predictability, and protection from arbitrary violence. This righteous facade served as an institutional fire extinguisher, absorbing the friction of his military expansion and generating a massive reserve of sociopolitical trust that effectively insulated his regime from the endemic rebellions that had plagued the Akkadian monarchs.

div.head: 5.3.3 The Hidden Fist: The Akitu and the E-Anna Engine
div.p: The brilliance of the Babylonian Synthesis lies in the fact that the righteous glove did not replace the Ishtarian fist; it merely concealed and regulated it. Despite his pious rhetoric, Hammurabi was an exceedingly ruthless military tactician. Over the course of his reign, he systematically dismantled his former allies—including the powerful Zimri-Lim of Mari—employing espionage, betrayal, and overwhelming martial force to unify MesopotamiaDominique Charpin, Hammurabi of Babylon (London: I.B. Tauris, 2012), pp. 45-62. Charpin meticulously details the Machiavellian diplomacy and brutal military campaigns that contradicted the king's pacifying public ideology..

To sustain the morale and mimetic loyalty of the standing army required to execute these campaigns, the E-Anna engine remained indispensable. Hammurabi's participation in the annual Akitu festival, and his structural integration into the ideology of the hieros gamos with Ishtar, provided the necessary charismatic hyper-valorization to bind and motivate his troops. However, this ideological continuity was expressed publicly in ways that differed markedly from the Ur III version. A significant literary shift has been documented by Assyriologists, including Samuel Noah Kramer, who famously noted that the passionate, explicitly sexual hieros gamos poetry, which was aggressively publicized under Ur III kings like Shulgi, fades from the public monumental record during the Old Babylonian period.See Samuel Noah Kramer, The Sacred Marriage Rite: Aspects of Faith, Myth, and Ritual in Ancient Sumer (Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1969), pp. 85-103. Kramer details the decline of the public Dumuzi-Inanna royal hymns, observing that the ritual became more institutionalized and less poetically overt. The overt public worship of Inanna-Ishtar was toned down as well, but her function as the bloody patroness of the military was absolutely retained. When the glove comes off in the epilogue of his Code, Hammurabi does not invoke Shamash to handle his military rivals; he explicitly unleashes the fury of Inanna-Ishtar:

cit.quote: May Inanna, the lady of battle and conflict, who bares my weapons, my gracious protecting spirit, who loves my reign, curse his kingdom in her angry heart, and in her great wrath, change his grace into evil! May she shatter his weapons on the field of battle and conflict, and create confusion and revolt for him!
cit.bibl: Martha T. Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1995), p. 138.

div.p: The goddess still granted Hammurabi martial-erotic fitness to rule. However, unlike Sargon, he did not broadcast this Ishtarian relationship as his sole or even primary justification for sovereignty. The fist remained functionally active on the battlefield and in the esoteric cultic sphere, but it was rigorously filtered through the public-facing administrative legitimacy of Marduk and Shamash. Consequently, the mimetic contagion of the warband was harnessed for conquest, while the newly subjugated populations were immediately pacified and reassured by the reliable imposition of Kullaba-style jurisprudence.

div.head: 5.4 [4] The Indo-Iranian Dynamic — Trifunctionality as Thermodynamic Tension
5.4.1 Reinterpreting the Trifunctional Hypothesis
div.p:
The temporal dynamics of the trifunctional Indo-European structure have been infrequently investigated. When Georges Dumézil introduced the notion in Jupiter, Mars, Quirinus
Georges Dumézil, Jupiter, Mars, Quirinus: Essai sur la conception indo-européenne de la société et sur les origines de Rome (Paris: Gallimard, 1941).
, he focused on one frozen snapshot: the vestigial functions of the three Roman flamines. Thereafter, in Dumézil's own works and those of his followers, the approach remained mostly the same: a series of equally static, generally also somewhat frozen and vestigial, snapshots. This is inherent in the tools used by the Dumézilian school: philology. We believe that the model introduced in Chapter 4 enables us to adopt a more dynamic approach. Given the state of our sources, this is not possible everywhere. In Northern European Celtic, Balto-Slavic, and Germanic contexts, the evolution of mythology is mostly lost, while in Southern Europe (Greece and Rome), the Middle-Eastern cultural influence is too pronounced to enable us to perceive much of the IE heritage of these cultures, apart from some of the few vestigial snapshots pointed out by Dumézil (the three flamines, the first three legendary kings of Rome, and so on). In only one area, the eastern Indo-Iranian domain, do we possess enough diachronic elements to investigate the dynamic dimension of the PIE religious-cultural structure. This is what we are going to focus on here, with a few limited excursuses into the Bronze Age Levant.

When applying the dual sovereignty model, specifically to its Indo-Iranian IE branch—before it stabilized into major territorial kingdoms such as the Kuru-Panchala state—the static structuralism of the Dumézilian triad must be reinterpreted as a state of dynamic, thermodynamic tension. In this schema, the PIE trifunctional structure mirrors the early Urukian model: the First Function (the juridical and cosmic sovereignty of the priests) maps directly to the Kullaba paradigm, acting as a regulating and stabilizing force fundamentally reliant on paternal linguistic prestige. The Second Function (the martial force of the Männerbund or ✶kóryos) maps identically to the E-Anna paradigm, operating as a transgressive engine fueled by a localized mimetic contagion of martial-erotic violence. Crucially, the Third Function (the agricultural and pastoral base) is not merely a passive provider of wealth; it constitutes the vast demographic reservoir from which the First Function periodically extracts a coalition of the meek to isolate, dilute, and ultimately sedate the explosive energy of the Second Function.

div.head: 5.4.2 Phase 1: The Central Asian Expansion and the BMAC Encounter
div.p: During their initial expansion into the steppes of Central Asia, the yet undifferentiated proto-Indo-Iranian groups operated under a relatively balanced, albeit primitive, formulation of this tripartition. Their theological apparatus centered on an inherited divine triad: the paternal sky god ✶Dyā́wš pitā́ (embodying the Kullaba/First Function), the martial thunder deity ✶Parkūnya (embodying the E-Anna/Second Function), and a formulation of the divine horse twins, the ✶Nasatya (representing the Third Function)The asterisk (✶) preceding these theonyms denotes that they are reconstructed linguistic forms rather than directly attested historical names. For comprehensive backgrounds on these Proto-Indo-European reconstructions and their later reflexes (such as the Rigvedic Parjanya for ✶Parkūnya), see J. P. Mallory and Douglas Q. Adams, The Oxford Introduction to Proto-Indo-European and the Proto-Indo-European World (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2006); Martin L. West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007); and Calvert Watkins, How to Kill a Dragon: Aspects of Indo-European Poetics (New York: Oxford University Press, 1995).. As these highly mobile pastoralists migrated southward, they encountered the sedentary, urbanized Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC)For an overview of the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex and its socio-economic interactions with nomadic pastoralists, see David W. Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language: How Bronze-Age Riders from the Eurasian Steppes Shaped the Modern World (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2007), pp. 421-435.. An initial phase of symbiotic interaction ensued, characterized by the trading of pastoral resources—specifically milk products and horses—in exchange for BMAC grain. This trade effectively enriched the Third Function, providing the demographic and material stability necessary for the pastoralists' Kullaba-aligned elders to maintain internal social cohesion and enforce diplomatic trust.

div.head: 5.4.3 Phase 2: The BMAC Borrowing and the ✶Wárunas Reform
div.p:
However, the influx of wealth and the proximity to affluent urban settlements inevitably disrupted the tribal equilibrium. A new generation of highly aggressive warbands began to coalesce around a newly elevated, volatile martial deity heavily influenced by, or directly borrowed from, BMAC religious constructs: ✶Índras For the linguistic argument that the theonym Índras represents a non-Indo-European loanword derived from the BMAC cultural sphere, see
Michael Witzel, Linguistic Evidence for Cultural Exchange in Prehistoric Western Central Asia, Sino-Platonic Papers 129 (2003): 1-70.
. ✶Índras was not a completely new god. He largely recycled ✶Parkūnya's old lore, with some syncretistic local elements, under a new name. Driven by the contagious, testosterone-fueled mimetic engine of this new BDMB archetype, these disruptive warbands engaged in extensive depredations. The traditional invocation of the ancient ✶Dyā́wš pitā́ proved sociopsychologically ineffective at containing this localized martial fever, as the archaic sky father lacked the immediate, terrifying gravity required to sedate the Männerbund.

In response to this existential thermodynamic crisis, a group of charismatic poet-priests—the ✶kavi On the evolution and socio-religious function of the visionary poet-priest (✶kavi) in Indo-Iranian tradition, see
Prods Oktor Skjærvø, Zarathustra: First Poet-Sacrificer, in Paitimāna: Essays in Iranian, Indo-European, and Indian Studies in Honor of Hanns-Peter Schmidt, ed. Siamak Adhami (Costa Mesa: Mazda Publishers, 2003), pp. 157-194.
—engineered a profound theological reform. To counteract the terrifying charisma of ✶Índras, they reformulated the ancient ✶Dyā́wš pitā́ lore, crystallizing a far more severe, omniscient paternal deity of cosmic order: ✶Wárunas. To reinforce this new Kullaba apparatus, ✶Wárunas was explicitly paired with ✶Mitrás, an existing god of oaths and contracts. By federating the terrified agriculturalists and traders under this reinforced, terrifyingly righteous paternal umbrella, the ✶kavi successfully generated a coalition of the meek large enough to temporarily quarantine the ✶Índras-worshiping warbands, stabilizing the region for several centuries. In our view, it is this religious reform which synthesized the specifically Indo-Aryan branch out of the broader Indo-Iranian ethnicity.

div.head: 5.4.4 Phase 3: The Collapse in Central Asia and the Indus Valley
div.p: This stability proved transitory. By the early second millennium BCE, a massive recrudescence of unruly, ✶Índras-centric warbands overwhelmed the mitigating capacities of the ✶Wárunas-aligned priesthood. The resulting epidemic of arbitrary martial violence completely eroded the security of the inter-regional trade routes upon which the BMAC and Indus Valley urbanized civilizations depended.

cit.quote: The Aryan warbands, glorifying the destruction of enclosures and the theft of cattle under the aegis of Indra, effectively rendered the ancient trade routes of Central Asia economically unviable, precipitating a cascading structural collapse across the broader region.
cit.bibl: Bernard Sergent, Genèse de l'Inde (Paris: Payot, 1997), p. 164.

div.p: Deprived of the vital flow of luxury goods, tin, and other commodities required to sustain their complex redistributive economies, both the BMAC and the Indus Valley civilizations, similarly dependent on the uninterrupted flow of commerce, underwent systemic and irreversible collapse. The pure E-Anna contagion had effectively annihilated the structural trust requisite for complex urbanism.

div.head: 5.4.5 Phase 4: The Gathic Revolution in the Hindu Kush
div.p:
Fleeing this apocalyptic outbreak of unalloyed E-Anna violence, a faction of visionary ✶kavi, accompanied by urban survivors and cattle herders from the collapsed BMAC network, sought refuge in the isolated, steep valleys of the Hindu Kush. It was within this traumatized crucible that the prophet Zarathustra The historical existence and precise dating of Zarathustra remain subjects of intense scholarly debate. We operate under the assumption that Zarathustra, akin to other foundational religious figures, is largely a composite construction synthesizing genuine historical elements from disparate periods. For discussions of this historiographical controversy, see
Jean Kellens, Essays on Zarathustra and Zoroastrianism (Costa Mesa: Mazda Publishers, 2000) ; and
Mary Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism, Vol. 1: The Early Period (Leiden: Brill, 1975).
initiated a radical theological revolution. His very name, possessing a strong BMAC linguistic flavor that explicitly incorporates the word for camel (uštra)—a regional beast of burden utterly antithetical to the warband's horse—signals his deep alignment with the sedentary and pastoral Third Function. Zarathustra birthed the Gathic theology by elevating a super-✶Wárunas, Ahura Mazda (an ahura/asura like ✶Wárunas), to a position of supreme, unchallengeable singularity.

Crucially, this revolution involved the absolute and permanent rejection of the martial E-Anna gods—including ✶Índras and the ✶Nasatya—classifying them collectively as daiva, malignant demonic entities of the Lie (druj). By utterly demonizing the charismatic engine of the warband, Zarathustra engineered a super-coalition of the meek governed exclusively by the absolute righteousness of cosmic truth. This pure Kullaba system successfully banished the Second Function from the realm of the sacred, evolving into history's first recorded monotheizing religion, Zoroastrianism. Ethnically, this initially Indo-Aryan religious group dissolved into subsequent Proto-Iranian waves moving into the Hindu Kush and beyond. The version of the Gathas we possess today is composed in the language of these later waves, in a dialect still remarkably close to Rigvedic Indo-Aryan Sanskrit.

div.head: 5.4.6 Phase 5: The Indo-Aryan Expansion and the Vrātya
div.p: In parallel with the Zoroastrian divergence, other descendant groups from the former BMAC sphere trickled south-eastward into India. These factions maintained the older, trifunctional theology comprising Varuna-Mitra, Indra, and the Nasatya (which we now mention with their Rigvedic names). However, the internal thermodynamic balance had shifted decisively: Varuna's influence was rapidly shrinking, effectively eclipsed by the hypertrophied martial prestige of Indra. Concurrently, the First Function priesthood compensated for Varuna's decline by elevating Agni, the god of the sacrificial fire, as their primary cultic and logistical anchor.

Within this context, the E-Anna warband remained terrifyingly central to the political structure, a reality vividly attested by the Battle of the Ten Kings documented in the Rigveda. As these groups established sedentary village life in the fertile Gangetic plain, the Kavi-Brahmin priesthood managed the endemic violence of the martial youth through a highly ritualized mechanism closely resembling the ver sacrum. They orchestrated the periodic, structural expulsion of the vrātya—the feral bands of young, unmarried warriors devoted to Indra and the nascent storm-god Rudra. A livable, village-centric sedentary life was maintained by instructing these vrātya bands to seek their cattle-raiding fortunes outside the established boundaries of their native village. Incidentally, this served as the primary kinetic instrument driving the aggressive expansion of the Indo-Aryans to the East.

Simultaneously, other detached warbands from this cultural matrix had previously moved westward across the Iranian Plateau, eventually forging the chariot-riding aristocracy of the Mitanni Empire and various smaller Levantine states in the Late Bronze Age. The deep-seated, systemic centrality of their raiding ethos is explicitly preserved in the dynastic names of some of their rulers—such as Biryawaza and Shattiwaza—which incorporate the lexeme vāja (meaning booty or martial prize). The triad Varuna-Mitra, Indra, Nasatya famously appears in the Boğazköy treaty The names of the Indo-Aryan deities Mitra, Varuna, Indra, and the Nasatya appear as divine witnesses in the treaty between the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I and the Mitanni king Shattiwaza. See
Paul Thieme, The Aryan Gods of the Mitanni Treaties, Journal of the American Oriental Society 80, no. 4 (1960): 301-317.
, establishing unambiguously that its Mitannian maryannu signatories were Indo-Aryans. Interestingly, the god Agni is not mentioned in this source nor in Maryannu personal names, probably indicating that the Levantine Indo-Aryans split away from the bulk of their relatives relatively early.

div.head: 5.4.7 Conclusion: The Perpetual Erosion and the Eventual Hindu Synthesis
div.p: In conclusion, the socio-religious evolution of the Proto-Indo-Iranians represents a continuous, evolving tussle between the Second Function (the martial-erotic warband) and the First Function (the juridical, paternal priesthood), constantly catalyzed by the fluctuating capacity of the Third Function to serve as a thermodynamic coolant coalition of the meek. This relentless structural friction resulted in the perpetual obsolescence and replacement of the First Function gods as their fire extinguisher capabilities were exhausted: the sky father ✶Dyā́wš pitā́ was superseded by the terrifying ✶Wárunas, who was in turn marginalized by the ritualistic Agni. This evolution continued through the esoteric abstractions of the Prajapatis, ultimately culminating in the historical Hindu synthesis under the stabilizing, world-preserving avatars of Vishnu.

In parallel, the violent E-Anna engine of the Second Function experienced a similar evolutionary drift: originating with ✶Parkūnya (remembered as Parjanya in the Rigveda), it violently morphed into the all-consuming ✶Índras. As Indra was gradually domesticated into an institutionalized royal figure, the raw martial contagion migrated to the terrifying Rudra, then to the destructive wind god Vayu, before finally achieving its mature, paradoxical synthesis as the world-destroying and world-generating ascetic, Shiva For a comprehensive analysis of the explicit sexual symbolism of the linga and yoni, and the theological pairing of Shiva with the dynamic, martial-erotic energy of the Ishtaric goddess (shakti) and her fierce avatars (such as Durga and Kali), see
Wendy Doniger O'Flaherty, Śiva: The Erotic Ascetic (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1981), pp. 20-45.
. The enduring architecture of historical Hinduism, therefore, represents the ultimate Indic stabilization of the Kullaba and the E-Anna—a cosmological equilibrium ensuring that neither the paternal ledger nor the martial-erotic sword could permanently obliterate the other.

div.head: 5.4.8 Addendum: ✶kóryos ritual group sex
div.p: A striking and gruesome manifestation of this dynamic is famously preserved in the 10th-century Arabic travelogue of Ahmad ibn Fadlan. Documenting the funeral of a Rus (Viking) chieftain on the Volga River, Ibn Fadlan describes a horrific, highly ritualized sequence wherein a doomed slave girl volunteers to accompany her master in death. Before her execution, she is subjected to a communal sexual rite with the men of the camp. As Ibn Fadlan vividly recounts in his Risala:

cit.quote: They made a tent over the ship... Then the men came with their shields and sticks. She was given a cup of nabidh [beer?]; she sang over it and drank it... Then men entered the tent and each one had sexual intercourse with the girl. Then they laid her at the side of her master; two held her feet and two her hands; the old woman known as the Angel of Death placed a rope around her neck... and she stabbed her with a broad-bladed dagger.
cit.bibl: Ahmad ibn Fadlan, Ibn Fadlan and the Land of Darkness: Arab Travellers in the Far North, trans. Paul Lunde and Caroline Stone (London: Penguin Books, 2012), pp. 50-51.

div.p: Throughout the Indo-European expansion area, from the Celtic fringes of Ireland to the eastern steppes bordering northern China, there are persistent accounts of brothers marrying a single wife or engaging in some kind of structured, communal sexual rites. These practices are either documented by neighboring, civilized observers or preserved as fossilized mythical forms in later religious texts. For example, Julius Caesar recorded that British Celtic bands of ten to twelve men—precisely the size of an archaic raiding party—shared wives among themselves. Similarly, Chinese chronicles such as the Weishu and the records of Sima Qian documented fraternal polyandry among the Yuezhi and their descendants, noting that a single wife would add horns to her headdress to signify the number of brothers she served. Furthermore, there are numerous accounts of barbarians having public sex in various forms, such as Herodotus's records of the Agathyrsi openly sharing women. In the realm of mythology, the most glaring literary fossil is Draupadi, the shared wife of the five Pandava brothers in the Indian Mahabharata, an epic survival that later orthodox Brahmin commentators desperately attempted to sanitize.

Nowadays, modern historiography tends to dismiss these widespread accounts as recycled anti-barbarian tropes, but this dismissal is more a reflection of institutional hyper-specialization than of any genuine historiographic concern. As is often the case, the big picture remains entirely out of reach for contemporary academia, which prefers to sanitize the past by treating these accounts as mere literary inventions designed to exoticize the other. However, when analyzed comparatively, these diverse pieces of evidence indicate quite convincingly the broad existence of ritual collective sex among the various iterations of the ancient ✶kóryos warband. Scholars who have recognized the structural reality of this archaic Indo-European youth brotherhood—such as Stig Wikander, Georges Dumézil, Alf Hiltebeitel, Kris Kershaw, and David W. AnthonyFor foundational scholarship recognizing the ✶kóryos as a transgressive warrior brotherhood, see Stig Wikander, Der arische Männerbund (Lund: Ohlsson, 1938); Georges Dumézil, Mythe et Épopée I. L'Idéologie des trois fonctions dans les épopées des peuples indo-européens (Paris: Gallimard, 1968); Alf Hiltebeitel, The Ritual of Battle: Krishna in the Mahābhārata (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1976); Kris Kershaw, The One-eyed God: Odin and the (Indo-)Germanic Männerbünde (Washington, D.C.: Journal of Indo-European Studies, 2000); and David W. Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language: How Bronze-Age Riders from the Eurasian Steppes Shaped the Modern World (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2007).—argue that these liminal fraternities lived outside of normal societal laws, engaging in ecstatic and transgressive rites to build absolute, unbreakable cohesion. It is this dreadful cohesion that is the main engine of the evolution described above.

The persistence of avoiding jealousy between brothers, cited as a motivation in many of these ancient sources, is particularly telling. By sharing sexual access, the warband actively averted a mimetic crisis that could tear the group apart. Herodotus explicitly provides this sociological logic when describing the Agathyrsi nomads, noting they shared women so that they may all be brothers... and not feel envy or hatred toward one another. Similarly, the Mahabharata acknowledges that the eldest Pandava mandated the sharing of Draupadi specifically to prevent the brothers from turning on each other out of lust.The narrative rationale for sharing Draupadi to prevent fraternal strife is explicitly detailed in the Adi Parva of the Mahabharata, where Yudhishthira observes his brothers lusting after her and mandates polyandry to avoid jealousy. Furthermore, this epic configuration operates as a humanized reflex of a much older mythic template found in the Rigveda. There, the Maruts—a roving, violent troop of young storm-warriors (marya) acting as a unified brotherhood—are invariably accompanied on their chariot by a single, shared female companion named Rodasī, acting as the unifying feminine axis and shared spouse for the entire divine fraternity. In a highly lethal, exiled brotherhood, exclusive sexual attachment is fatal; it breeds the exact mimetic rivalry that destroys fraternal bonds, as seen in the foundational conflicts between Romulus and Remus or Cain and Abel.

Crucially, we do not consider this institution as particularly or uniquely archaic in its Indo-European form. In all probability, the ✶kóryos sexual rite is a nomadic, highly mobile adaptation of the older Urukian proto-hieros gamos rites. These dynamics likely emerged in the early military subculture that coalesced in the course of the early fourth millennium BCE around the earliest tavern-brothels on Earth in Uruk. The deep antiquity and structural necessity of this transgressive energy is perfectly encoded in Sumerian mythology: when the goddess Inanna steals the me (the divine decrees of civilization) from the patriarchal god EnkiFor the myth of Inanna and Enki, detailing her transfer of the me to Uruk, including the decrees of sexual intercourse and prostitution, see Samuel Noah Kramer and John Maier, Myths of Enki, The Crafty God (New York: Oxford University Press, 1989), pp. 57-68. and brings them to Uruk, prostitution is explicitly included in the sacred list of civilization-building powers.

In all these instances, the E-Anna engine relies on the transgressive dismantling of sexual exclusivity to forge the lethal, uncompromising solidarity of the warband—a dynamic that the Kullaba priesthoods would spend subsequent millennia attempting to domesticate or suppress. The modern collegiate McThelema has not invented anything; it has merely regressed to the level of our most ancient PIE rituals.

div.head: 5.5 [5] The Indo-European Royal Synthesis
5.5.1 The Indic Royal Synthesis: Kuru-Panchala
div.p: As established in the preceding analysis of Proto-Indo-European dynamics, the nomadic phase of Indo-Aryan expansion was characterized by the violent, outward-facing centrifugal energy of the vrātya warbands (or Männerbund). However, the transition to territorial, sedentary statehood—epitomized by the emergence of the Kuru-Panchala kingdom in the Iron Age—necessitated the profound domestication of this pure martial contagion. Within this newly consolidated realm, the martial sovereign transitioned from the feral chieftain into the formalized institution of Hindu kingship.

In the Indic sphere, this structural morphing was operationalized through highly complex orthopraxic rituals, most notably the rājasūya (royal consecration) and aśvamedha (horse sacrifice). During these rites, the king was systematically stripped of his arbitrary warlord persona and structurally subordinated to the Brahmin priesthood. The king retained his martial monopoly (the E-Anna fist, represented by his identification with Indra), but his capacity to wield it was explicitly circumscribed by the overarching dictates of dharma, administered exclusively by the Kullaba-aligned priests. As J. C. Heesterman has demonstrated, the Indian synthesis achieved stability through deliberate ritual separation; the king is left mimetically powerful but ritually impure, permanently dependent on the Brahmin for cosmic legitimation.See J. C. Heesterman, The Inner Conflict of Tradition: Essays in Indian Ritual, Kingship, and Society (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1985), pp. 108-115.

cit.quote: The emergence of the Kuru realm is of extraordinary importance as its civilization has influenced later Indian ritual, society and political formations, frequently even until today.
cit.bibl: Michael Witzel, Early Sanskritization: Origins and Development of the Kuru State, in Electronic Journal of Vedic Studies (Kyoto: EJVS, 1995), p. 2.

div.head: 5.5.2 The Celtic Banais Ríghi
div.p: At the extreme western periphery of the Indo-European expansion, in Ireland, the structural morphing of trifunctionality into royal ideology preserved an astonishingly overt manifestation of the Ishtarian engine. The inauguration of the Celtic king was explicitly conceptualized as a sacred marriage, the banais ríghi (royal wedding). In this framework, the prospective sovereign was required to symbolically mate with the territorial goddess of sovereignty—frequently manifesting as terrifying, martial-erotic figures such as Medb or the Mórrígan.

This iteration is a practically unmodified survival of the hieros gamos dynamic observed in ancient Babylon. The goddess confers the raw, physical fitness to rule, effectively transferring the E-Anna’s charismatic surplus to the monarch. However, the druid First Function maintained regulatory control by strictly evaluating the king’s adherence to fír flathemon (the ruler's truth, functionally equivalent to the Rigvedic Ṛta and to the Iranic Aṣ̌a). If the king’s martial-erotic engine was not properly balanced by this Kullaba-style righteous justice, the land itself would ostensibly reject him, turning barren.

cit.quote: The sacral king is the spouse of his kingdom and his inauguration ceremony is known as banais righi, wedding-feast of kingship; in other words he is then ritually united with the sovereignty of the territory over which he rules... The sexual element is almost always present...
cit.bibl: Proinsias Mac Cana, Celtic Mythology (London: Hamlyn, 1970), p. 117.

div.p: To what extent the Druidic royal synthesis was comparable to the Brahmanical one is difficult to determine, given the dissimilarity of our sources. The medieval monks who wrote about the banais ríghi did not particularly care for the intricacies of Druidic rituals, and they certainly did not want to foreground the role of their direct predecessors in the First Function.For a comprehensive analysis of how pre-Christian Celtic mythology and Druidic traditions were transmitted, sanitized, and systematically altered by medieval Christian clerics, see Kim McCone, Pagan Past and Christian Present in Early Irish Literature (Maynooth: An Sagart, 1990). Be that as it may, it is clear that the trifunctional structure was strictly isomorphic.

div.head: 5.5.3 The Anatolian Synthesis: Hittite Kingship
div.p: In Anatolia, the Hittite kingdom successfully established a highly durable territorial state. The Hittite monarch (tabarna) operated explicitly as the chief priest and supreme judicial administrator of the realm, channeling the paternal order of the Storm God Tarḫunna and the Sun Goddess of Arinna. This authority was structurally mediated by the panku—the assembly of nobles which functioned as a Kullaba-esque regulating body, alongside the powerful tawananna (Great Queen).

Yet, during periods of acute dynastic crisis, the latent E-Anna engine was abruptly reactivated to secure charismatic legitimacy. This is spectacularly evident in the usurpation of Hattusili III and his queen, Puduhepa. Lacking the legal, Kullaba-based dynastic right to the throne, Hattusili violently seized power and explicitly justified his illegal coup by invoking the overwhelming, personal favor of Šauška of Šamuḫa (the Hurro-Hittite iteration of Ishtar). Like Sargon of Akkad before him, the usurper utilized the terrifying, unmediated martial-erotic prestige of the goddess to bypass established legal constraints.For Hattusili III's usurpation justified by divine martial favor, see Trevor Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2005), pp. 250-254.

div.head: 5.5.4 The Early Roman Monarchy
div.p: The structural ideology of the early Roman monarchy represents one of the most pristine historical distillations of the Indo-European tripartite system morphing into an institutionalized state, a dynamic famously decoded by Georges Dumézil. The first three legendary kings of Rome are not mere historical figures, but anthropomorphized embodiments of the thermodynamic engine of sovereignty:

cit.quote: The first function, sovereignty, has two sides, one frenetic and magical, the other juridical and regulated... represented by the first two kings, Romulus and Numa respectively. The second function, military force, is represented by the third king, Tullus.
cit.bibl: Georges Dumézil, Jupiter, Mars, Quirinus: Essai sur la conception indo-européenne de la société et sur les origines de Rome (Paris: Gallimard, 1941), pp. 79-82.

list.item: Romulus and Numa Pompilius (First Function/Kullaba): Romulus embodies the terrifying, magical aspect of pure sovereignty (aligned with Jupiter, or the Indic Varuna), while Numa represents its juridical, priestly, and stabilizing counterpart (aligned with Fides, or the Indic Mitra). Together, they establish the paternal laws and linguistic trust of the state.

Tullus Hostilius (Second Function/E-Anna): A pure manifestation of raw martial violence (aligned with Mars). His reign is entirely consumed by aggressive military expansion (including the destruction of Alba Longa) and the terrifying, unbridled contagion of the warband, ultimately ending in his literal incineration by a lightning bolt when he fails to properly execute the Kullaba's rituals. This story is evidently narrated by a Kullaba-aligned voice, reminding us that the Ishtarian energy must be contained.

Ancus Marcius (Third Function): The synthesizer who focuses on plebeian prosperity, infrastructure, and the demographic mass (aligned with Quirinus, or the Indic Nasatya) required to permanently ground the energies of the preceding kings.

div.head: 5.5.5 The Republican Rupture: A Zoroastrian Echo in Rome
div.p: The delicate trifunctional balance of the early Roman monarchy ultimately collapsed under the Etruscan dynasty, culminating in the reign of Tarquinius Superbus. Tarquin governed as a pure, unalloyed E-Anna tyrant—a martial sovereign who bypassed the Kullaba-aligned Senate and relied entirely on coercive terror and centralized charismatic excess. The subsequent revolution that expelled the kings and birthed the Roman Republic was not merely a political coup; it was a profound theological rupture that structurally mirrors the monotheizing reforms of Zarathustra.

Just as Zarathustra permanently rejected the martial-erotic ✶daiva to construct a super-coalition of the meek based on pure cosmic truth, the Roman patricians violently rejected the Ishtarian engine of kingship. The mythological catalyst for this revolution—the rape of Lucretia—is highly diagnostic. It represents the ultimate structural repudiation of the E-Anna's transgressive sexual prestige. The tyrant's son, Sextus Tarquinius, violating the pristine domesticity of the Third Function (Lucretia) proves that the martial-erotic contagion had become an existential threat to societal order.

cit.quote: Sextus Tarquin... pressed his left hand on the woman's breast and said, Be still, Lucretia! I am Sextus Tarquin. My sword is in my hand. Utter a sound, and you die! [...] When he saw that she was resolute and not to be moved even by the fear of death, he threatened to disgrace her memory... by this terrifying prospect his lust became victorious.
cit.bibl: Titus Livius, Ab Urbe Condita (Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1919), p. 201.

div.p: The ideological purge effected by the republican transition is corroborated by the archaeological record. Following the revolution, the archaic Sant'Omobono temples—dedicated to Fortuna and Mater Matuta, goddesses deeply associated with Etruscan royal fertility, female charismatic power, and the legacy of the king Servius Tullius (who heavily syncretized them with Astarte)—were deliberately and violently destroyed.

cit.quote: The abandonment of the site at Sant'Omobono contributes to the general impression of an oligarchic coup against a populist tyranny.
cit.bibl: Tim J. Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome: Italy and Rome from the Bronze Age to the Punic Wars (London: Routledge, 1995), p. 240.

div.p: In place of the charismatic warlord, the Romans engineered a pure, puritanical Kullaba state. Power was aggressively decentralized into the hands of the Senate and annually elected magistrates. The Republic’s ideological foundation was exclusively grounded in mos maiorum (the custom of the ancestors) and pietas (strict, bloodless devotion to duty, family, and the gods). This pure Apollonian system successfully banished the martial-erotic sovereign from the Roman psyche for half a millennium, until the massive influx of wealth and standing armies during the late Republic caused the E-Anna contagion to irresistibly resurface in the persons of Julius Caesar and Mark Antony.
